questions.question: From the alternatives given below, choose the correct meaning of the idiom 'to be chuffed to bits'.

options.text: To be very sad or gloomy
To be very happy or pleased
To shatter the heart to bits

questions.solution: The correct answer is: **To be very happy or pleased**. **__Key Points__** __ • The idiom **'to be chuffed to bits'** is a **British colloquial expression** used to describe someone who is extremely pleased, delighted, or proud of a particular outcome. (बहुत प्रसन्न या खुश होना) • **Example: **I was **chuffed to bits** when I found out that I had passed my final exams with such high marks. • **'To be very happy or pleased'** is the literal interpretation of the idiom, signifying a high state of **joy** and **satisfaction**. (बहुत खुश या प्रसन्न होना) • **Example: **The team was **very happy or pleased** to receive the championship trophy after months of hard work. • Hence, we can infer that the meaning of the idiom **'to be chuffed to bits'** is to be very happy. questions.question: From the alternatives given below, choose the correct meaning of the idiom 'a flea in one's ear'.

questions.question:
Select the correct alternative to fill in the blank with the correct preposition in the following sentence. 

A few people dislike earning money ____ unfair means.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is '**by**'. **__Key Points__** __ 
• The preposition '**by**' is used to identify the **method**, **means**, or **agency** through which an action is performed. 
• The phrase '**by unfair means**' is a common idiomatic expression used to indicate that someone is using **dishonest** or **unethical** ways to achieve a result. 
• In the context of **earning money**, '**by**' correctly connects the action to the method used. 
• **Options 2, 3,** and **4** do not fit grammatically or idiomatically with the word '**means**' in this sentence structure. Therefore, the correct answer is **Option 1**. **Complete Sentence:** *'A few people dislike earning money **by**__ unfair means.'* **__Additional Information__** 
• **Option 2: 'on'** is generally used to denote **position** on a surface or **specific days** and dates. 
• **Option 3: 'in'** is used for **enclosed spaces**, **geographic locations**, or **months/years**. 
• **Option 4: 'for'** typically indicates **purpose**, **duration**, or **reason**. </ul

questions.question:
Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into Passive Voice? 

The conservation team has saved several endangered species this year.

options.text: Several endangered species are saved by the conservation team this year.
Several endangered species were saved by the conservation team this year.
Several endangered species had been saved by the conservation team this year.
Several endangered species have been saved by the conservation team this year.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Several endangered species have been saved by the conservation team this year.**__.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• The given sentence is in the **Active Voice** and uses the **Present Perfect Tense**. The structure follows: **Subject + has/have + Past Participle (V3) + Object**.
 
• In the original sentence, **The conservation team** is the **Subject**, **has saved** is the **Verb**, and **several endangered species** is the **Object**.
 
• To convert a **Present Perfect** sentence into **Passive Voice**, the structure used is: **New Subject (Original Object) + has/have + been + Past Participle (V3) + by + New Object (Original Subject)**.
 
• The phrase **several endangered species** is **plural**; therefore, the auxiliary verb **have** must be used instead of **has** to maintain **Subject-Verb Agreement**.
 
• The **Past Participle** form of the verb **save** is **saved**, which remains the same in the passive construction.
 
• The **adjunct of time**, **this year**, is placed at the end of the sentence to maintain the original meaning and flow.

 **Additional Information__**

 
• Review of incorrect options based on **Tense**:
 
 
• **Simple Present Passive**: Uses **is/am/are + V3**. Option 1 is incorrect because it changes the **Present Perfect** to **Simple Present**.
 
• **Simple Past Passive**: Uses **was/were + V3**. Option 2 is incorrect because it shifts the tense to the **Past**.
 
• **Past Perfect Passive**: Uses **had been + V3**. Option 3 is incorrect because it uses the **Past Perfect** tense instead of **Present Perfect**.
 
 
 
• General Rule for **Passive Voice**:
 
 
• The **Subject** and **Object** interchange their positions.
 
• The preposition **by** is typically used before the **agent** (the doer of the action).
 
• The **Passive Voice** always requires a form of the verb **to be** followed by the **Past Participle**.
 
 
</ul

questions.question:
Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into Passive Voice? 

Will she have submitted her thesis before mine is?

options.text: Will her thesis be submitted by her before mine is?
Will her thesis have been submitted before mine is?
Will her thesis been submitted by her before mine is?
Will her thesis submitted by her before me is?

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Will her thesis have been submitted before mine is?**__.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• The original sentence is in the **Future Perfect Tense** in its **Interrogative** form. The active voice structure for this tense is: **Will + Subject + have + V3 (Past Participle) + Object?**
 
• To convert a sentence from the **Future Perfect Active** to **Passive Voice**, the structure must change to: **Will + Object (as new subject) + have been + V3 + (by + Subject)?**
 
• In the provided sentence, **she** is the **Subject**, **submitted** is the **Verb**, and **her thesis** is the **Direct Object**.
 
• During conversion, the object **her thesis** moves to the front of the sentence (after the auxiliary **Will**), and the verb phrase **have submitted** transforms into **have been submitted**.
 
• The phrase **before mine is** functions as an **Adverbial Clause of Time** and remains unchanged in the passive construction.
 
• In **Passive Voice**, the agent (**by her**) is often omitted if the focus is entirely on the action or the object, which is consistent with the most grammatically accurate option provided.

 **Additional Information__**

 
• Analysis of incorrect options:
 
 
• **Option 1** is incorrect because it uses the **Future Indefinite Passive** structure (**be submitted**) instead of the **Future Perfect**.
 
• **Option 3** is grammatically flawed as it omits the auxiliary verb **have**, which is required before **been** in the perfect tense.
 
• **Option 4** is incorrect because it lacks the necessary auxiliary verbs **have been** and uses incorrect syntax in the terminal clause.
 
 
 
• **Voice Conversion Rules**:
 
 
• The **Past Participle** form of the verb is mandatory in all passive voice sentences.
 
• The **Tense** of the sentence must never change during the transformation from active to passive.
 
• In **Interrogative** sentences, the **Auxiliary Verb** (Will) must remain at the beginning of the sentence to maintain the question format.
 
 
</ul

questions.question:
Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into active voice?

Let the guests not be kept waiting at the gate.

options.text: Don't keep the guests waiting at the gate.
The guests don't keep waiting at the gate.
You mustn't be kept waiting the guests at the gate.
The guests should not keep waiting at the gate.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Don't keep the guests waiting at the gate.**__.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• The provided sentence is a **Negative Imperative** sentence currently in the **Passive Voice**. The grammatical structure of such sentences usually follows the pattern: **Let + Object + not + be + V3 (Past Participle)**.
 
• In this sentence, **the guests** is the **Direct Object**, **not** is the negative particle, and **kept** is the **Past Participle** of the verb **keep**.
 
• To convert a negative imperative from **Passive to Active Voice**, the word **Let** and the auxiliary verb **be** are removed. The sentence must then begin with the negative auxiliary **Don't** (or **Do not**) to maintain the imperative mood.
 
• In the **Active Voice**, the verb must return to its **Base Form (V1)**. Therefore, the participle **kept** is transformed back into the root verb **keep**.
 
• The final structure for the active conversion is: **Don't + Base Verb + Object + Complement**. Following this rule results in: **Don't keep the guests waiting at the gate**.

 **Additional Information__**

 
• **Imperative Mood and Voice**:
 
 
• **Imperative Sentences** are used to convey commands, requests, or prohibitions. In these sentences, the subject **You** is always implied but rarely explicitly stated in the **Active Voice**.
 
• In **Active Voice**, a positive command starts directly with the verb (e.g., **Keep the gate shut**), whereas in **Passive Voice**, it typically starts with **Let** (e.g., **Let the gate be kept shut**).
 
 
 
• **Transformation of Negation**:
 
 
• In the **Active Voice**, the prohibition is signaled by **Don't** at the beginning of the sentence.
 
• In the **Passive Voice**, the word **not** is positioned between the object and the auxiliary **be**. Incorrect options often fail to maintain this specific relationship or alter the **tense** and **mood** of the sentence.
 
 
</ul

questions.question:

Tina must apologize ______ Ravi for her misbehaviour.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is '**to**'. **__Key Points__** __ 
• The verb **apologize** is commonly used with the preposition **to** when it refers to the **person** receiving the apology. 
• The general grammatical structure followed is: **apologize + to + someone + for + something**. 
• In the given sentence, **Ravi** is the person being apologized to, so the preposition **to** is required to complete the phrase correctly.

• **Option 2: 'for'** is used to indicate the **reason** for the apology (e.g., apologize **for** the delay), which already appears later in the sentence (**for** her misbehaviour). 
• **Option 4: 'al'** is not a standard English preposition and is grammatically irrelevant. </ul

questions.question:
A part of the following sentence is underlined. Choose the option that can replace the underlined part to improve the sentence. In case Options A, B and C are not found suitable, choose Option D: "No Improvement Required."

 

The prestigious award was given to the scientist for his groundbreaking research in genetics.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**groundbreaking research in genetics**__.

**__Key Points__**

__
 
• The term **groundbreaking** is a **compound adjective** that characterizes **scientific research** or **pioneering discoveries** that represent a significant **innovation**; it metaphorically refers to **breaking new ground** in a specific **academic discipline**.
 
• **Genetics** is the **biological science** that studies **heredity**, **genes**, and **genetic variation** in organisms; the term was formally coined by the **British biologist William Bateson** in **1905**.
 
• In **formal English**, **research** is typically treated as an **uncountable noun**, and the **prepositional phrase** **in genetics** correctly identifies the **scientific field** or **domain** of the **scientist's** work.
 
• The **original sentence** is **grammatically sound** as the word **groundbreaking** is the most **idiomatic** and **formal** choice for describing **award-winning research**, making this phrase the **correct choice** for the sentence.

 **Additional Information__**

 
• **Groundshaking and Genetic**
 
 
• **Groundshaking**: This **adjective** usually describes **literal seismic activity** (earthquakes) or **metaphorical shocks** that cause **great surprise**, but it is not the standard **collocation** used for **academic research**.
 
• **Genetic**: This is an **adjectival form** (e.g., **genetic engineering**); when referring to the **entire field of study**, the **noun** **genetics** (with the **-ics** suffix) must be used.
 
 
 
• **Common Errors**
 
 
• **Orthographic Errors**: Terms like **groundbraking** are **misspellings**; **braking** refers to **slowing down a vehicle**, while **breaking** refers to **shattering** or **opening** something.
 
 
</ul

questions.question:
Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.

S1. The walls were filled with pictures and calendars.

A. "That's Mr. Connin," Mrs. Connin said, standing back from the stove for a second to admire the face with him, "but it don't favor him anymore."

B. He had long hair and a gold circle around his head and he was sawing on a board while some children stood watching him.

C. Bevel turned from Mr. Connin to a coloured picture over the bed of a man wearing a white sheet.

D. There were two round photographs of an old man and woman with collapsed mouths and another picture of a man whose eyebrows dashed out of two bushes of hair and clashed in a heap on the bridge of his nose; the rest of his face stuck out like a bare cliff to fall from.

S2. He was going to ask who that was when the three boys came in again and motioned for him to follow them.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **Option 4**.

 

**__Key Points__**

 
• **Sentence S1** is the fixed starting sentence which introduces the setting: **the walls were filled with pictures and calendars**. 
• **Sentence D** is the second sentence as it provides a detailed description of the various **photographs and pictures** mentioned in S1, specifically describing an old couple and a man with bushy eyebrows. 
• **Sentence A** follows D because **Mrs. Connin** identifies the man described in the previous sentence as **Mr. Connin**, commenting that the picture does not look like him anymore. 
• **Sentence C** is the fourth sentence as it describes the protagonist, **Bevel**, turning his attention away from Mr. Connin to a **different coloured picture** located over the bed, featuring a man in a white sheet. 
• **Sentence B** follows C by providing the visual details of the man in the **white sheet**, mentioning **long hair**, a **gold circle** (halo), and the act of **sawing on a board**. 
• **Sentence S2** is the fixed concluding sentence which explains that Bevel was about to ask about the identity of the man in the carpentry scene when he was interrupted. 
• The correct sequence is **DACB**. 

 

**Coherent paragraph after rearrangement**:

'The walls were filled with pictures and calendars. There were two round photographs of an old man and woman with collapsed mouths and another picture of a man whose eyebrows dashed out of two bushes of hair and clashed in a heap on the bridge of his nose; the rest of his face stuck out like a bare cliff to fall from. 'That's Mr. Connin,' Mrs. Connin said, standing back from the stove for a sec to admire the face with him, 'but it don't favor him anymore.' Bevel turned from Mr. Connin to a coloured picture over the bed of a man wearing a white sheet. He had long hair and a gold circle around his head and he was sawing on a board while some children stood watching him. He was going to ask who that was when the three boys came in again and motioned for him to follow them.'</div

• The passage is a narrative written in the **past tense**, as indicated by the opening phrase '**It was a rainy evening**'. 
• The sequence of events follows a specific timeline in the past. After '**It was a rainy evening**', the next action is that **Rohan** got onto the bus. 
• To describe a completed action in the past, we use the **Simple Past Tense**. The simple past form of the verb 'board' is '**boarded**'. 
• The following sentence uses the past perfect '**had just finished**', which supports the context that the entire story is set in the past. Therefore, the correct answer is '**Option 2**'. Complete Passage: *It was a rainy evening when Rohan 1. boarded__ a crowded city bus. He had just finished his tuition classes and was eager to reach home. As he searched for his ticket, he 2. __suddenly__ realized his wallet was missing. His heart began to race. Had he dropped it, or had someone stolen it? 'Don’t panic, think carefully,' he told himself. He remembered using the wallet 3. __at__ a small tea stall near the bus stop. Could it still be there? What if someone else had already picked it up? When the bus stopped at the next signal, Rohan quickly got down. 'Please hurry, I must go back!' he whispered under his breath. He ran in the rain, splashing through puddles, his mind full of fear and hope. To his surprise, the tea vendor smiled and said, 'Young man, you left this behind.' He held out the wet but safe wallet. What a 4. __relief__ it was! Rohan almost shouted with joy. He thanked the vendor again and again. This small 5. __incident__ taught Rohan a big lesson. He realized that not everyone in the world is dishonest, and kindness often appears when least expected. As he walked home in the rain, he thought, 'I will never be careless with my belongings again!'* **__Additional Information__** 
• '**Board**' is the base form/present tense, which does not match the established past tense of the story. 
• '**Boards**' is the third-person singular present tense; it is grammatically incorrect for a past narrative. 
• '**Has boarded**' is the **present perfect tense**, used for actions that happened at an unspecified time or have current relevance, which does not fit a story describing specific past events.
